input.rationale: Turning to the configuration and participant eligibility mechanism, which the earlier questions did not touch, I noticed a mismatch between AddVoter's documented contract and what the code does: the captured comment says the given server is added as a staging server that the leader promotes once it is ready, while the configuration change installs it as a Voter immediately. If the documented workflow (add first, start later) is what an operator follows, then adding a server that is not yet running changes the commit quorum at once, and when the living voters are fewer than the new quorum the cluster can neither commit nor elect. This submission registers that question and submits a two-case probe: an unreachable address added to a single-voter cluster and to a three-voter cluster, with the resulting configuration, quorum, apply outcome, leader state and whether the same API can remove the server again. Native feedback from the local dry run, explicitly not retained evidence, is the reason this is worth a receipt: on the single-voter cluster the added server appeared as a Voter, the leader stepped down without any leader being elected afterwards, applies and removal both came back as not-leader, and the config still listed two voters; on the three-voter cluster the same steps left the leader in place, applies succeeded and removal succeeded.

investigations.question: Does AddVoter install the new server as a Voter immediately, in contrast to its documented staging behaviour, so that adding a server that is not yet running can leave a cluster unable to commit or to elect, and unable to undo the change through the same API?
investigations.hypothesis: AddVoter's comment promises that the server is added as a staging server and promoted once it is ready, but nextConfiguration's AddVoter branch builds the new Server with Suffrage Voter, and Staging is deprecated and unused, so the change takes effect as a full membership change as soon as it is committed. When the number of living voters is below the resulting quorum - for example a single-voter cluster that adds one unreachable server - the leader can no longer contact a quorum, steps down through its lease check, and the cluster has no way back through the API because an election needs the same quorum and config changes require a leader.
investigations.discriminator: Add an address that no transport answers through the exported AddVoter API, on a single-voter cluster and on a three-voter cluster, and record the resulting configuration (the added server's suffrage and the quorum), whether a subsequent apply succeeds, whether any leader exists afterwards, and whether RemoveServer for the added server succeeds. The hypothesis predicts failure of apply and removal with no leader on the single-voter cluster, and unremarkable success on the three-voter cluster where the living voters still satisfy the quorum.

scope.description: Two cases over real clusters with the in-memory transport: a single-voter cluster and a three-voter cluster, each healthy and committing before the change. In each case the harness records a baseline apply, adds a server address that no transport answers through the exported AddVoter API, records the resulting configuration (voters, the added server's suffrage, the quorum and whether the quorum exceeds the living voters), then attempts an apply and reports whether it succeeded, which state the node is in and how many leaders the cluster has, and finally attempts RemoveServer for the added server and reports whether that succeeded and what the configuration lists afterwards.
assumptions: The added server is represented by a freshly created in-memory transport address that is never connected to the cluster, so no peer can answer it; this is the state of a server that has not been started yet.

The documented workflow under test is the one AddVoter's comment describes - add the server, then bring it up - so the probe follows the documentation rather than inventing a use the API does not describe.

Captured in-memory timeouts are used, so the lease and election timers are the ones the target's own tests run with, and each future is waited for with a bound and reported as resolved or not rather than assumed.
excluded: No on-disk store, no network transport and no multi-process execution; the added server is never started, which is the premise of the case rather than an omission.
The probe does not test the promotion path the documentation describes, because no such path exists in the captured code to test.

investigations.question: Does NewRaft complete when RestoreCommittedLogs replays a large committed-but-unapplied window, and if not, which mechanism prevents completion?
investigations.hypothesis: NewRaft blocks permanently inside the startup replay once the replay window contains more than 128*MaxAppendEntries FSM-bound entries: processLogs sends FSM batches on the 128-slot fsmMutateCh, and the only consumer, runFSM, is started later in the same NewRaft call, so no goroutine can ever drain the buffer and the caller has no Raft handle with which to trigger shutdown.
investigations.discriminator: Restart the same real single-voter node over unchanged stores and vary only the size of the replay window (committed entries above the last snapshot) and MaxAppendEntries. The hypothesis predicts non-return exactly when the window's FSM-bound entries exceed 128*MaxAppendEntries (blocked stack ending in the replay send), and return for windows below that, with the window and batch counts reported as observed operands.

knowledge.assertion: The startup replay delivers FSM batches by blocking send on fsmMutateCh before runFSM exists.
Non-return follows from FSM-bound window entries exceeding 128*MaxAppendEntries.

investigations.question: Can a TimeoutNow message that no longer reflects the current leader start an election that displaces a live leader, given that the handler clears the receiver's known leader, moves it to Candidate, sets candidateFromLeadershipTransfer, and the resulting RequestVote waives the 'we have a leader' rejection on other servers?
investigations.hypothesis: TimeoutNowRequest carries only the RPC header and no term, and raft.timeoutNow performs no term comparison, no check that the sender is the current leader and no membership check: it clears the leader, sets Candidate and marks the candidacy as coming from a leadership transfer, and requestVote on other servers then grants the vote even though the voter knows a live leader and is not in a transfer of its own. Election safety (term, one vote per term, log freshness) is preserved, so the question is scoped to authority/liveness: whether a TimeoutNow that a leader produced before losing leadership can still be delivered and displace a healthy current-term leader.
investigations.discriminator: Trace the real producer path (initiateLeadershipTransfer -> leadershipTransfer -> trans.TimeoutNow) and the consumer path (processRPC -> timeoutNow -> runCandidate with candidateFromLeadershipTransfer, then requestVote's LeadershipTransfer bypass) and identify which permitted event in the captured snapshot can deliver the request after the receiving node learned a newer leader. A real interrupted transfer in a small cluster should then show the receiver entering candidacy and peers granting votes despite a live leader, while a control where the transfer completes before the leadership change should not.

investigations.question: If a leadership transfer is interrupted while its drain loop still has replication work, can the transfer goroutine be stranded on the followerReplication triggerDeferErrorCh send so that the deferred setLeadershipTransferInProgress(false) never runs, leaving a node that later becomes leader permanently rejecting client operations with ErrLeadershipTransferInProgress?
investigations.hypothesis: The drain loop sends a deferError on repl.triggerDeferErrorCh outside any arm on the transfer's stop channel, and the only reader of that channel is the peer's replication goroutine, which exits when the leader steps down (runLeader's defer closes its stopCh) or when the peer is removed. If the leader loses leadership between the goroutine's wake-up and that send, the send has no reader and blocks forever; the outer transfer goroutine then blocks on doneCh before its deferred setLeadershipTransferInProgress(false), so the flag stays set for the lifetime of the Raft instance, including after a later election of that instance.
investigations.discriminator: Run a real three-voter cluster, isolate the transfer target, commit a backlog that the target never receives, start a transfer to that target, then cut the starting leader off so it steps down while the transfer is draining. Predict: the transfer future resolves with an error, the drained goroutine is left in the triggerDeferErrorCh send, getLeadershipTransferInProgress stays true, and after the old leader is made leader again through a normal transfer its Apply and GetConfiguration return ErrLeadershipTransferInProgress. A control trial without the interruption must show the flag cleared and client calls unaffected; if every interrupted trial clears the flag with no stranded goroutine, the hypothesis is defeated for this trigger.

investigations.question: Does VerifyLeader confirm leadership using acknowledgements that do not count toward the voter quorum, so that a leader separated from every other voter but still able to reach a nonvoter reports itself verified?
investigations.hypothesis: verifyLeader seeds votes with the leader's own vote and registers the verify future with every followerReplication in leaderState.replState, which startStopReplication creates for every server in the latest configuration including nonvoters; each successful AppendEntries response then calls notifyAll, which casts a vote for every registered future. Since quorumSize counts only voters, acknowledgements from nonvoters can complete the voter quorum, so a leader whose only reachable peers are nonvoters returns a successful VerifyLeader while it cannot contact a majority of voters - and while another leader may already have been elected among the voters it cannot reach.
investigations.discriminator: Run a real cluster of three voters plus one nonvoter, elect the leader, confirm it can verify normally, then partition the leader together with the nonvoter away from the other two voters and call VerifyLeader on the leader before the new term reaches the nonvoter. Predict: the future returns nil with votes counting only the leader's own vote plus the nonvoter's acknowledgement, while the leader's configurations.latest contains three voters, so the confirmation is made against a quorum of voters it cannot reach; a control in which the nonvoter is also cut off must fail the verification instead.

investigations.question: On a leader that has lost contact with every other voter but can still reach a nonvoter, for how long do verifications keep succeeding relative to the moment the detached voters elect their own leader and commit entries - does the confirmation window overlap a competing leader, or does the leader's own lease end it first?
investigations.hypothesis: Because checkLeaderLease counts only voters, the cut-off leader keeps confirming only until its lease check steps it down, which is one LeaderLeaseTimeout after its last successful contact with a voter; the detached voters' election starts from their own heartbeat timeouts. With the captured relations between those timers the confirmation window may close before a competing leader appears, in which case the defect is confined to the confirmation primitive - an unsound confirmation while no competing leader yet exists - rather than to an observed stale read.
investigations.discriminator: Partition the leader together with the nonvoter on a real three-voter plus one-nonvoter cluster, poll the exported verification path while it is confirmable, record the last successful confirmation's elapsed time, then watch until the detached voters report a leader and record when that happens and whether it precedes or follows the last confirmation. Overlap (a competing leader before the last confirmation) would support a stale-read consequence; a clean separation would narrow it. The control, with the nonvoter cut off too, must produce no confirmations at all.

scope.description: Five restart-only cases over the real hashicorp/raft single-voter node (in-memory transport, real commit-tracking log store): produce a committed log with the actual leader, stop the node, then call NewRaft again over the unchanged stores with a fresh transport on the same address, and record whether NewRaft returns. Cases vary only the size of the committed-but-unapplied startup replay window (applies before the restart, plus an optional manual snapshot before shutdown) and MaxAppendEntries.
assumptions: RestoreCommittedLogs=true with a CommitTrackingLogStore, which is the documented opt-in configuration for this feature.

Automatic snapshotting is disabled (SnapshotThreshold=math.MaxUint64, SnapshotInterval=1h) so the replay window is set explicitly instead of by timer; this models a node whose newest snapshot lags its commit index, which the default 120s SnapshotInterval plus 8192 SnapshotThreshold also produce at higher write rates.
Restarted instances are constructed with a null logger so that no logging occurs after the test completes; logging is not part of the observed mechanism.
The bounded 5s wait is not the evidence: a returning restart is expected to be ~ms, and the blocked case is additionally recorded as a goroutine stack in the startup replay path.
excluded: Multi-voter clusters, network faults, and on-disk (bolt) log stores are excluded; the mechanism observed is in the startup replay path, not in replication.
The FSM's own semantics are excluded: MockFSM only records applied logs, and no FSM behavior is asserted.

basis.prefix: Each case builds one real single-voter cluster with opts{Peers:1, Bootstrap:true, CommitTrackingLogs:true} so the log store, stable store, snapshot store and FSM are produced by the target itself: the leader dispatches and commits the applied commands through the normal leaderLoop/dispatchLogs path, which stages the commit index via StageCommitIndex and stores the entries. Before shutdown the harness reads the store's persisted commit index, the last log index, cap(fsmMutateCh), the configured MaxAppendEntries, and censuses the entry types in the replay window with GetLog using the same rule as Raft.prepareLog. For the snapshot case it takes a user snapshot before shutdown and uses that snapshot's index as the restart's last-applied point. It then calls leader.Shutdown(), creates a fresh NewInmemTransport on the same address, and calls NewRaft over the unchanged logs/stable/snapshots instances as the target's own restart tests do, in a goroutine that reports completion through a channel; the harness waits up to 5s and, if nothing arrived, samples all goroutine stacks and keeps the one on the startup replay path. No production code is modified; the harness only reads state and drives the exported lifecycle.

scope.description: Twelve trials (ten interrupted, two control) over real three-voter clusters with the in-memory transport: in the interrupted trials the transfer target is isolated, a backlog is committed that the target never receives, a leadership transfer to that target is started, and the starting leader is then isolated so it steps down while the transfer still has replication work; the partition is healed, the rest of the cluster elects, and the interrupted node is made leader again through a normal transfer so its client entry points can be exercised.
assumptions: In-memory transport with the captured in-memory timeouts (50ms heartbeat/election/lease), so the interruption and step-down happen within milliseconds; this is the same facility the target's own tests use.

LeadershipTransferToServer is the documented client contract for starting a transfer; isolating the leader is a permitted environment event, and the target's step-down follows from its own lease check.
In the control trials the same transfer runs with no interruption and no backlog, so a trial-level difference is attributable to the interruption rather than to the transfer itself.
The observed flag and state are read through the same in-package accessors the target's own tests use; the client-visible endpoints are Apply and GetConfiguration.
excluded: No on-disk log store, no network transport and no multi-process execution: the mechanism under test is the transfer goroutine's interaction with leadership loss, not storage or sockets.
No attempt is made to widen the race window artificially, for example by pausing goroutines or by modifying production code.

It records both last indexes, starts a transfer to the target with LeadershipTransferToServer, waits 30ms so the drain loop is running, then isolates the starting leader so that it loses quorum contact and steps down while the transfer still has work. scope.description: Two trials over real four-voter clusters with the in-memory transport: one voter is demoted to nonvoter with DemoteVoter, the leader is verified while healthy, and then in the interrupted trial the leader is partitioned together with the nonvoter while in the control trial the leader is partitioned alone. Reachability is not claimed from the contact timestamps: the leader-side suffrages are a property of the partition the harness applied, reported as such, and the observation that the other voters could not reach the leader is carried by their own election and commit.
Votes and quorum are read through the same in-package accessors the target's own tests use; the verification itself is driven through the same channel the exported VerifyLeader API uses.
excluded: No on-disk store, no network transport and no multi-process execution.
No injection of a synthetic request: every event comes from the target's own leader loop, replication goroutines and exported APIs.

result.summary: With the two earlier findings consolidated, I moved to the configuration and participant eligibility mechanism, which nothing so far had touched, and found a contract mismatch worth a probe: AddVoter's captured comment says the given server is added as a staging server that the leader promotes once it is ready, while the AddVoter branch of nextConfiguration builds the new server with Suffrage Voter immediately, and Staging is deprecated and unused. Following the documented workflow — add the server, then bring it up — therefore changes the commit quorum at once, which in the adverse case leaves a cluster unable to commit, and for a single-voter cluster also unable to elect and unable to undo the change. The probe submits exactly that comparison: an address no transport answers is added through the exported AddVoter API to a single-voter cluster and to a three-voter cluster, and the events separate the applicability (the added server's suffrage, the voter count, the quorum, and whether the quorum exceeds the living voters) from the measured outcome (whether a later apply succeeded, the node's state, how many leaders remain, and whether RemoveServer for that server succeeded). Three comparisons declare the prediction, the control where the living voters still satisfy the quorum, and the claim that no in-band repair exists. Native feedback from the local dry run, explicitly not retained evidence: on the single-voter cluster the added server appeared as a Voter, the node ended as a Candidate with no leader in the cluster, and both the apply and the removal came back as not-leader with the configuration still listing two voters, while on the three-voter cluster the same steps left the leader in place with applies and removal succeeding. I also corrected one derived operand before submitting so the applicability reflects the quorum rather than a bare voter-count comparison.

investigations.question: Does NewRaft complete when RestoreCommittedLogs replays a large committed-but-unapplied window, and if not, which mechanism prevents completion?
investigations.hypothesis: NewRaft blocks permanently inside the startup replay once the replay window contains more than 128*MaxAppendEntries FSM-bound entries: processLogs sends FSM batches on the 128-slot fsmMutateCh, and the only consumer, runFSM, is started later in the same NewRaft call, so no goroutine can ever drain the buffer and the caller has no Raft handle with which to trigger shutdown.
investigations.discriminator: Restart the same real single-voter node over unchanged stores and vary only the size of the replay window (committed entries above the last snapshot) and MaxAppendEntries. The hypothesis predicts non-return exactly when the window's FSM-bound entries exceed 128*MaxAppendEntries (blocked stack ending in the replay send), and return for windows below that, with the window and batch counts reported as observed operands.

knowledge.assertion: The startup replay delivers FSM batches by blocking send on fsmMutateCh before runFSM exists.
Non-return follows from FSM-bound window entries exceeding 128*MaxAppendEntries.

investigations.question: Can a TimeoutNow message that no longer reflects the current leader start an election that displaces a live leader, given that the handler clears the receiver's known leader, moves it to Candidate, sets candidateFromLeadershipTransfer, and the resulting RequestVote waives the 'we have a leader' rejection on other servers?
investigations.hypothesis: TimeoutNowRequest carries only the RPC header and no term, and raft.timeoutNow performs no term comparison, no check that the sender is the current leader and no membership check: it clears the leader, sets Candidate and marks the candidacy as coming from a leadership transfer, and requestVote on other servers then grants the vote even though the voter knows a live leader and is not in a transfer of its own. Election safety (term, one vote per term, log freshness) is preserved, so the question is scoped to authority/liveness: whether a TimeoutNow that a leader produced before losing leadership can still be delivered and displace a healthy current-term leader.
investigations.discriminator: Trace the real producer path (initiateLeadershipTransfer -> leadershipTransfer -> trans.TimeoutNow) and the consumer path (processRPC -> timeoutNow -> runCandidate with candidateFromLeadershipTransfer, then requestVote's LeadershipTransfer bypass) and identify which permitted event in the captured snapshot can deliver the request after the receiving node learned a newer leader. A real interrupted transfer in a small cluster should then show the receiver entering candidacy and peers granting votes despite a live leader, while a control where the transfer completes before the leadership change should not.

investigations.question: If a leadership transfer is interrupted while its drain loop still has replication work, can the transfer goroutine be stranded on the followerReplication triggerDeferErrorCh send so that the deferred setLeadershipTransferInProgress(false) never runs, leaving a node that later becomes leader permanently rejecting client operations with ErrLeadershipTransferInProgress?
investigations.hypothesis: The drain loop sends a deferError on repl.triggerDeferErrorCh outside any arm on the transfer's stop channel, and the only reader of that channel is the peer's replication goroutine, which exits when the leader steps down (runLeader's defer closes its stopCh) or when the peer is removed. If the leader loses leadership between the goroutine's wake-up and that send, the send has no reader and blocks forever; the outer transfer goroutine then blocks on doneCh before its deferred setLeadershipTransferInProgress(false), so the flag stays set for the lifetime of the Raft instance, including after a later election of that instance.
investigations.discriminator: Run a real three-voter cluster, isolate the transfer target, commit a backlog that the target never receives, start a transfer to that target, then cut the starting leader off so it steps down while the transfer is draining. Predict: the transfer future resolves with an error, the drained goroutine is left in the triggerDeferErrorCh send, getLeadershipTransferInProgress stays true, and after the old leader is made leader again through a normal transfer its Apply and GetConfiguration return ErrLeadershipTransferInProgress. A control trial without the interruption must show the flag cleared and client calls unaffected; if every interrupted trial clears the flag with no stranded goroutine, the hypothesis is defeated for this trigger.

investigations.question: Does VerifyLeader confirm leadership using acknowledgements that do not count toward the voter quorum, so that a leader separated from every other voter but still able to reach a nonvoter reports itself verified?
investigations.hypothesis: verifyLeader seeds votes with the leader's own vote and registers the verify future with every followerReplication in leaderState.replState, which startStopReplication creates for every server in the latest configuration including nonvoters; each successful AppendEntries response then calls notifyAll, which casts a vote for every registered future. Since quorumSize counts only voters, acknowledgements from nonvoters can complete the voter quorum, so a leader whose only reachable peers are nonvoters returns a successful VerifyLeader while it cannot contact a majority of voters - and while another leader may already have been elected among the voters it cannot reach.
investigations.discriminator: Run a real cluster of three voters plus one nonvoter, elect the leader, confirm it can verify normally, then partition the leader together with the nonvoter away from the other two voters and call VerifyLeader on the leader before the new term reaches the nonvoter. Predict: the future returns nil with votes counting only the leader's own vote plus the nonvoter's acknowledgement, while the leader's configurations.latest contains three voters, so the confirmation is made against a quorum of voters it cannot reach; a control in which the nonvoter is also cut off must fail the verification instead.

investigations.question: On a leader that has lost contact with every other voter but can still reach a nonvoter, for how long do verifications keep succeeding relative to the moment the detached voters elect their own leader and commit entries - does the confirmation window overlap a competing leader, or does the leader's own lease end it first?
investigations.hypothesis: Because checkLeaderLease counts only voters, the cut-off leader keeps confirming only until its lease check steps it down, which is one LeaderLeaseTimeout after its last successful contact with a voter; the detached voters' election starts from their own heartbeat timeouts. With the captured relations between those timers the confirmation window may close before a competing leader appears, in which case the defect is confined to the confirmation primitive - an unsound confirmation while no competing leader yet exists - rather than to an observed stale read.
investigations.discriminator: Partition the leader together with the nonvoter on a real three-voter plus one-nonvoter cluster, poll the exported verification path while it is confirmable, record the last successful confirmation's elapsed time, then watch until the detached voters report a leader and record when that happens and whether it precedes or follows the last confirmation. Overlap (a competing leader before the last confirmation) would support a stale-read consequence; a clean separation would narrow it. The control, with the nonvoter cut off too, must produce no confirmations at all.

investigations.question: Does AddVoter install the new server as a Voter immediately, in contrast to its documented staging behaviour, so that adding a server that is not yet running can leave a cluster unable to commit or to elect, and unable to undo the change through the same API?
investigations.hypothesis: AddVoter's comment promises that the server is added as a staging server and promoted once it is ready, but nextConfiguration's AddVoter branch builds the new Server with Suffrage Voter, and Staging is deprecated and unused, so the change takes effect as a full membership change as soon as it is committed. When the number of living voters is below the resulting quorum - for example a single-voter cluster that adds one unreachable server - the leader can no longer contact a quorum, steps down through its lease check, and the cluster has no way back through the API because an election needs the same quorum and config changes require a leader.
investigations.discriminator: Add an address that no transport answers through the exported AddVoter API, on a single-voter cluster and on a three-voter cluster, and record the resulting configuration (the added server's suffrage and the quorum), whether a subsequent apply succeeds, whether any leader exists afterwards, and whether RemoveServer for the added server succeeds. The hypothesis predicts failure of apply and removal with no leader on the single-voter cluster, and unremarkable success on the three-voter cluster where the living voters still satisfy the quorum.

scope.description: Five restart-only cases over the real hashicorp/raft single-voter node (in-memory transport, real commit-tracking log store): produce a committed log with the actual leader, stop the node, then call NewRaft again over the unchanged stores with a fresh transport on the same address, and record whether NewRaft returns. Cases vary only the size of the committed-but-unapplied startup replay window (applies before the restart, plus an optional manual snapshot before shutdown) and MaxAppendEntries.
assumptions: RestoreCommittedLogs=true with a CommitTrackingLogStore, which is the documented opt-in configuration for this feature.

Automatic snapshotting is disabled (SnapshotThreshold=math.MaxUint64, SnapshotInterval=1h) so the replay window is set explicitly instead of by timer; this models a node whose newest snapshot lags its commit index, which the default 120s SnapshotInterval plus 8192 SnapshotThreshold also produce at higher write rates.
Restarted instances are constructed with a null logger so that no logging occurs after the test completes; logging is not part of the observed mechanism.
The bounded 5s wait is not the evidence: a returning restart is expected to be ~ms, and the blocked case is additionally recorded as a goroutine stack in the startup replay path.
excluded: Multi-voter clusters, network faults, and on-disk (bolt) log stores are excluded; the mechanism observed is in the startup replay path, not in replication.
The FSM's own semantics are excluded: MockFSM only records applied logs, and no FSM behavior is asserted.

parameters.recorded_operands: persisted_commit_index, last_log_index, snapshot_index, last_applied_before_restart, replay_window, fsm_bound_entries_in_window (entry-type census using the prepareLog rule), max_append_entries, fsm_mutate_ch_capacity (read from the running instance), estimated_replay_batches, restart_returned, restart_elapsed_ms, restart_error, restart_stack_frames

basis.prefix: Each case builds one real single-voter cluster with opts{Peers:1, Bootstrap:true, CommitTrackingLogs:true} so the log store, stable store, snapshot store and FSM are produced by the target itself: the leader dispatches and commits the applied commands through the normal leaderLoop/dispatchLogs path, which stages the commit index via StageCommitIndex and stores the entries. Before shutdown the harness reads the store's persisted commit index, the last log index, cap(fsmMutateCh), the configured MaxAppendEntries, and censuses the entry types in the replay window with GetLog using the same rule as Raft.prepareLog. For the snapshot case it takes a user snapshot before shutdown and uses that snapshot's index as the restart's last-applied point. It then calls leader.Shutdown(), creates a fresh NewInmemTransport on the same address, and calls NewRaft over the unchanged logs/stable/snapshots instances as the target's own restart tests do, in a goroutine that reports completion through a channel; the harness waits up to 5s and, if nothing arrived, samples all goroutine stacks and keeps the one on the startup replay path. No production code is modified; the harness only reads state and drives the exported lifecycle.

scope.description: Seven restart-only cases over the real hashicorp/raft single-voter node (in-memory transport, real commit-tracking log store): produce a committed log with the actual leader, stop the node, then call NewRaft again over the unchanged stores with a fresh transport on the same address, and record whether NewRaft returns. Cases vary the size of the committed-but-unapplied startup replay window (applies before the restart, plus an optional manual snapshot before shutdown) and MaxAppendEntries, which together decide how many FSM batches the replay must place in the 128-slot fsmMutateCh.
assumptions: RestoreCommittedLogs=true with a CommitTrackingLogStore, the documented opt-in configuration for this feature.

Automatic snapshotting is disabled (SnapshotThreshold=math.MaxUint64, SnapshotInterval=1h) so the replay window is set explicitly instead of by timer; this models a node whose newest snapshot lags its commit index, which the default 120s SnapshotInterval plus 8192 SnapshotThreshold also produce when more than 8192 entries are committed between snapshot checks.
Restarted instances are constructed with a null logger so no logging occurs after the test completes; logging is not part of the observed mechanism.

A returning restart is expected in the millisecond range, and the 5s wait is a ceiling for recording non-return, not the evidence for it: the non-return cases are additionally recorded with the stack of the goroutine left in the startup replay path.

scope.description: Twelve trials (ten interrupted, two control) over real three-voter clusters with the in-memory transport: in the interrupted trials the transfer target is isolated, a backlog is committed that the target never receives, a leadership transfer to that target is started, and the starting leader is then isolated so it steps down while the transfer still has replication work; the partition is healed, the rest of the cluster elects, and the interrupted node is made leader again through a normal transfer so its client entry points can be exercised.
assumptions: In-memory transport with the captured in-memory timeouts (50ms heartbeat/election/lease), so the interruption and step-down happen within milliseconds; this is the same facility the target's own tests use.

LeadershipTransferToServer is the documented client contract for starting a transfer; isolating the leader is a permitted environment event, and the target's step-down follows from its own lease check.
In the control trials the same transfer runs with no interruption and no backlog, so a trial-level difference is attributable to the interruption rather than to the transfer itself.
The observed flag and state are read through the same in-package accessors the target's own tests use; the client-visible endpoints are Apply and GetConfiguration.
excluded: No on-disk log store, no network transport and no multi-process execution: the mechanism under test is the transfer goroutine's interaction with leadership loss, not storage or sockets.
No attempt is made to widen the race window artificially, for example by pausing goroutines or by modifying production code.

It records both last indexes, starts a transfer to the target with LeadershipTransferToServer, waits 30ms so the drain loop is running, then isolates the starting leader so that it loses quorum contact and steps down while the transfer still has work. After 300ms it heals the partitions, waits for a leader among the remaining nodes, reads the transfer flag through the in-package accessor, samples goroutine stacks for a goroutine left in the leadership transfer path, and finally makes the interrupted node leader again with a normal transfer from the current leader and calls Apply and GetConfiguration on it, recording the exact errors. Control trials run the transfer without any partition or backlog. Only the TestAssurance-prefixed test in this harness is selected and no production file is modified.

scope.description: Two trials over real four-voter clusters with the in-memory transport: one voter is demoted to nonvoter with DemoteVoter, the leader is verified while healthy, and then in the interrupted trial the leader is partitioned together with the nonvoter while in the control trial the leader is partitioned alone. Each trial records the verification outcome, the vote tally and the quorum it was measured against, the suffrages on the leader's side of the partition, and - for the interrupted trial - whether the voters the leader cannot reach elected their own leader and committed an entry that the interrupted leader never applied.
assumptions: The in-memory transport is used with the captured in-memory timeouts, so the leader lease and election timers are the same ones the target's own tests use; this keeps the verification inside the window before the interrupted leader's own lease check steps it down.
The demotion goes through the exported DemoteVoter contract, so the configuration that produces three voters plus one nonvoter is produced by the target rather than written into a store by hand.

Reachability is not claimed from the contact timestamps: the leader-side suffrages are a property of the partition the harness applied, reported as such, and the observation that the other voters could not reach the leader is carried by their own election and commit.
Votes and quorum are read through the same in-package accessors the target's own tests use; the verification itself is driven through the same channel the exported VerifyLeader API uses.
excluded: No on-disk store, no network transport and no multi-process execution.
No injection of a synthetic request: every event comes from the target's own leader loop, replication goroutines and exported APIs.

before.description: Two trials over real four-voter clusters with the in-memory transport: one voter is demoted to nonvoter with DemoteVoter, the leader is verified while healthy, and then in the interrupted trial the leader is partitioned together with the nonvoter while in the control trial the leader is partitioned alone. Each trial records the verification outcome, the vote tally and the quorum it was measured against, the suffrages on the leader's side of the partition, and - for the interrupted trial - whether the voters the leader cannot reach elected their own leader and committed an entry that the interrupted leader never applied.
assumptions: The in-memory transport is used with the captured in-memory timeouts, so the leader lease and election timers are the same ones the target's own tests use; this keeps the verification inside the window before the interrupted leader's own lease check steps it down.
The demotion goes through the exported DemoteVoter contract, so the configuration that produces three voters plus one nonvoter is produced by the target rather than written into a store by hand.

Reachability is not claimed from the contact timestamps: the leader-side suffrages are a property of the partition the harness applied, reported as such, and the observation that the other voters could not reach the leader is carried by their own election and commit.
Votes and quorum are read through the same in-package accessors the target's own tests use; the verification itself is driven through the same channel the exported VerifyLeader API uses.
excluded: No on-disk store, no network transport and no multi-process execution.
No injection of a synthetic request: every event comes from the target's own leader loop, replication goroutines and exported APIs.

scope.description: Two trials on real four-voter clusters with one voter demoted to nonvoter through DemoteVoter: the interrupted trial partitions the leader together with the nonvoter and the control partitions the leader alone. Each trial verifies the healthy leader, applies the partition, polls the exported verification path while the leader is still confirmable, keeps watching until the detached voters report their own leader, and reports the last confirmation's and the competing leader's elapsed times on the same clock together with the competing leader's commit index and the cut-off leader's applied index.
assumptions: Captured in-memory timeouts are used, so the lease and election relations are the ones the target's own tests run with; the leader lease is shorter than the election timeout in this configuration, which is a property of the configuration and is reported through the timeline rather than assumed.
The verification is driven through the same channel the exported VerifyLeader API uses, with a bounded wait per poll; polls stop as soon as the leader is no longer confirmable.

The competing leader is identified by which raft instance reports Leader among the two voters that were detached from the interrupted leader, and the observation window for it is 3s, which is longer than this cluster's election time.
excluded: No application-level read is served in this harness; the measurement is about the confirmation and the competing leader's existence, not about what an application would return.
No on-disk store, no network transport and no synthetic request injection.

scope.description: Two cases over real clusters with the in-memory transport: a single-voter cluster and a three-voter cluster, each healthy and committing before the change. In each case the harness records a baseline apply, adds a server address that no transport answers through the exported AddVoter API, records the resulting configuration (voters, the added server's suffrage, the quorum and whether the quorum exceeds the living voters), then attempts an apply and reports whether it succeeded, which state the node is in and how many leaders the cluster has, and finally attempts RemoveServer for the added server and reports whether that succeeded and what the configuration lists afterwards.
assumptions: The added server is represented by a freshly created in-memory transport address that is never connected to the cluster, so no peer can answer it; this is the state of a server that has not been started yet.

The documented workflow under test is the one AddVoter's comment describes - add the server, then bring it up - so the probe follows the documentation rather than inventing a use the API does not describe.

Captured in-memory timeouts are used, so the lease and election timers are the ones the target's own tests run with, and each future is waited for with a bound and reported as resolved or not rather than assumed.
excluded: No on-disk store, no network transport and no multi-process execution; the added server is never started, which is the premise of the case rather than an omission.
The probe does not test the promotion path the documentation describes, because no such path exists in the captured code to test.

basis.prefix: Each case builds a real cluster with MakeCluster and the captured in-memory timeouts, takes the elected leader, and creates a fresh in-memory transport address that is never connected to the cluster to stand for a server that has not been started. It confirms the cluster commits a command before the change, then calls the exported AddVoter with that address, waits for the returned future with a bound, and reads back the configuration to report the added server's suffrage, the number of voters, how many of them are living, and whether the quorum exceeds the living voters. After letting the lease timer run, it attempts an apply with a bounded wait and reports whether the future resolved, whether it succeeded, the error, the node's state and how many leaders the cluster has. Finally it attempts RemoveServer for the added server with a bounded wait and reports whether that succeeded and what the configuration lists afterwards. Only the TestAssurance-prefixed test in this harness is selected and no production file is modified.
